Therefore, the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
Just as when the great flow of water is exhausted, waves do not arise;
so too, when the mental consciousness ceases,
the various forms of consciousness do not arise.
That is called deluded consciousness;
it is taken as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The six kinds of objective consciousnesses (*viṣayavijñāna*) constitute the various consciousnesses.
This is because false consciousness is the root of the six [consciousnesses].
When the mind of false conceptualization ceases,
it causes those various six consciousnesses not to arise.
The relationship between the fundamental and the derivative within the false [nature] is thus.
Next, we shall distinguish the support solely from the perspective of the true [nature].
The true nature possesses both essence and function.
The fundamentally pure true mind is taught to be the essence;
it appears or disappears according to conditions.
It is taught that there must be function;
function necessarily depends upon a substance,
which is termed its "basis."
The essence is able to sustain function;
it is described as "sustaining" because it can sustain like water.
The dependent can be likened to waves;
the analogies of the rope and the snake, and so forth, are likewise the same.
Thus concludes this section on the mutual dependence and support of the real and the false.
Next, within the consciousness that is the common characteristic of both the real and the delusory,
the fundamental and the derivative are correlated to distinguish their mutual support:
the Real and Ignorance conjoin to constitute the Fundamental Consciousness.
Based on the fundamental storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the appropriating consciousness (ādānavijñāna) arises together with it;
based on that, the six types of evolving consciousnesses arise together.
Within this division:
The fundamental consciousness is the root;
the other two are the branches.
The branches arise depending upon the root.
This is termed "dependence.
The root is fundamentally able to sustain the branches,
causing them to flow and continue without interruption.
It is called "retention" (dhāraṇī) because it can sustain like water and can rely upon like waves.
Question: Within the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, it is stated that the *ādānavijñāna* arises simultaneously with the six consciousnesses.
Is there not the sense of mutual dependence and support between them?
Śāriputra replied:
"It is not permitted within this portion."
The six consciousnesses arise directly from the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
They are transformations of the fundamental consciousness;
their substance is the fundamental consciousness itself.
According to the *ālayavijñāna*, it is said to be the support (*āśraya*) and the sustainer (*dhṛti*);
it is not that the *ādānavijñāna* transforms into the six consciousnesses,
for the substance of the six consciousnesses is not the *ādānavijñāna*.
Therefore, Vaibhāṣikas do not speak of a supporting basis (*āśraya*).
It is like when a person in a dream sees, hears, perceives, or cognizes;
these arise from the dreaming mind and do not arise from a grasping at a self within the dream.
If one speaks in terms of the causal basis,
it is also unobjectionable to say that [the aggregates] are "based upon" or "sustained by" [the self].
What is the meaning of this?
It is because, due to the grasping of the mind as "I" by the *ādāna* [consciousness],
it perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Not seeing the suchness of dharmas,
one does not realize nirvana; instead,
the six consciousnesses and the objects of the six sense organs arise through transformation.
Apart from these, it does not exist;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Because of attachment to a self."
Sentient beings in the world receive bodies;
apart from the self, there would be no activity.
From this meaning, it can be said that [the body] serves as a support.
Having completed the exposition of these two gates based on the support,
next follows the sixth gate,
which clarifies the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, distinguishing perfuming (*vāsanā*) by means of the specific characteristics of the true and the false consciousnesses;
second, discussing perfuming by means of the common characteristics of the true and the false consciousnesses.
The preceding middle section is divided into three parts:
first, the essential nature of the dharma as perfumed;
second, a general explanation of the meaning of perfuming.
Third, the extensive explanation of the characteristics of perfuming.
Regarding the dharma of perfuming,
it is stated in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*:
It is said that there are four kinds:
first, the perfuming of pure dharmas,
which refers to suchness.
Second is the perfuming of the cause of defilement,
which is ignorance;
third is the perfuming of the deluded mind.
What is called "karmic consciousness" (karma-vijñāna) refers to everything from karmic consciousness up to the continuous [consciousness] within the seventh consciousness.
This is collectively termed the "karmic consciousness.
It is permeated by the four types of delusory objects,
namely, the false objects produced by the conceptualizing mind.
These four are still from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*:
"In this way, according to reality, the ignorant do not know and give rise to eight kinds of false conceptualization,
which produce two kinds of phenomena."
The permeation of True Suchness is like that reality itself;
ignorance is like the ordinary, deluded person who does not know it.
The deluded mind is like that which gives rise to the eight kinds of false conceptualization;
the deluded objects are like those produced within the three matters, specifically the first:
the matter of falsehood. Question:
Regarding the objective consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*) and its objective bases—the sense organs and their objects—why are they not said to be perfumed (*vāsita*)?
Because this category arises from that which has not yet been perfumed, it is not so described. This concludes this section.
Next is the second section,
which generally elucidates perfuming (*vāsanā*),
as explained in the treatise.
As for the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*):
just as a garment that has no fragrance is made to have one through perfuming,
so too is it with the mind.
In reality, there is no defilement;
it is through the perfuming of delusion that it appears to exist.
In delusion, there is no purity.
Because true perfuming causes [the unreal] to exist,
within that state of delusion,
there can arise the practice of skillful means as an antidote.
The commentary has thus concluded these two sections.
Next, the characteristics of perfuming (vāsanā) will be explained in detail.
First, the arising of defilement is clarified.
The subsequent section clarifies the arising of purity.
Within the context of the arising of defilement,
there are two distinct meanings.
First, the sequence of the mutual arising of perfuming (*vāsanā*) is clarified based on the preceding four dharmas;
second, the differences in what is produced by perfuming are specifically explained.
Regarding the meaning of their mutual arising:
As stated in the treatise:
because one relies upon the first true suchness (tathatā),
there arises the second cause of defilement, which is ignorance.
Because there is the cause of the defiled dharma of ignorance,
it perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness), whereby a deluded mind arises.
It is like a person whose retributive mind is shrouded by deep sleep, whereby a dreaming mind arises.
Because the deluded mind perfumes ignorance,
one fails to understand that True Suchness is quiescent and equal; thus,
awakening does not occur and thought arises.
Thereupon, false objects arise;
it is like a person whose dreaming mind is stirred, causing them to emerge from deep sleep into the realm of dreams.
Because these false objects exist, [the mind continues to function].
The perfumed and agitated deluded mind then gives rise to conceptual attachment and creates various kinds of karma.
They undergo various kinds of suffering.
"Recollection" (nian) is like craving (ai);
"attachment" (zhu) is like seeing (jian).
In this matter, the consciousness, views, craving, afflictions, the creation of karma,
and the experience of suffering all arise based on delusion;
their manifestation is thus.
Next, the differences arising from perfuming (vāsanā) are explained.
As stated in the treatise:
"Seeking the root from the branches."
This shall be explained in sequence.
There are two types [of consciousness] arising from the habitual perfuming of delusory objects:
first, that which increases discursive thought (*vāsanā*).
"Recollection" (*smṛti*) is like craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
"The increase of grasping" (*upādāna-vardhana*)—
grasping (*upādāna*) is like views (*dṛṣṭi*).
That which arises from the perfuming of the deluded mind is also twofold.
First, the fruit of transformation arising from perfuming;
this refers to the experience of the subtle suffering of the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
Second, it gives rise to the fruit of segmented existence (*paricchinna-phala*),
meaning that one undergoes the coarse suffering of the segmented existence of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
This occurs because the power of continuity within deluded consciousness sustains and maintains all karmas.
Because one attains that fruit,
there are likewise two [aspects] arising from the permeation of ignorance:
first, ignorance deludes and obscures the true mind.
Permeated by false conditioning,
they form false seeds within false consciousness.
Second, because the true mind is deludedly obscured by ignorance,
it receives the perfuming of good and evil,
thereby forming the seeds of phenomena.
It arises from the consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñāna*).
That which is produced by the perfuming of *tathatā* is also twofold:
first, it gives rise to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Second, the arising of deluded mind:
because that True Suchness (tathatā) is free from discrimination,
it can give rise to ignorance (avidyā).
Because its nature is that of awareness,
when it is shrouded by delusion,
a false mind arises.
Just as when a person grasps the mind as being of the nature of cognition,
and it is then shrouded by昏睡 (torpor and sleep),
dream-cognition arises.
The arising of defilement is thus.
Next, the arising of purity is explained.
There are two types of the arising of purity.
First, the true [nature] perfumes the deluded;
second, the deluded perfumes the true.
Within the perfuming of the true upon the deluded:
First, the perfuming agent is explained;
subsequently, the perfumable object is explained.
There are two types of perfuming agents.
First, the perfuming of the true essence;
second, the perfuming of the true function.
Regarding the perfuming of the essence:
As stated in the treatise:
from beginningless time,
it possesses the nature of untainted dharmas and inconceivable karmic activity.
The perfuming of the deluded mind enables sentient beings to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death and to joyfully seek nirvana;
it causes them to have confidence that their own bodies possess the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, thereby inspiring them to resolve upon practice and cultivation.
The fundamental substance of the Dharma-body is called the untainted dharma (anāsrava-dharma).
This is the primary designation for the Reward Buddha (saṃbhoga-buddha).
This is called the nature of performing activity.
These two are also analyzed in detail within the section on the meaning of Buddha-nature.
It is by virtue of these two that [the following occurs].
"The capacity to permeate is illusory.
He asked:
"If it is the True that can permeate the illusory to give rise to wholesome practice,"
All sentient beings possess *tathatā* (suchness) equally;
why then do they not all undergo uniform permeation so that they may simultaneously resolve their minds and initiate the practices of cultivation?
They enter into nirvāṇa;
yet among sentient beings,
there are immeasurable distinctions of superior and inferior, and of prior and subsequent, regarding their faith and lack thereof.
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"True Suchness is fundamentally one,
yet the afflictions of sentient beings vary in thickness."
There are differences between them;
therefore, their relative superiority and inferiority are not equal.
Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, there are causes and conditions.
Only when these two are complete can [the result] be accomplished;
it is like fire, which, though its nature exists within wood, [cannot manifest without conditions].
People must crowd together to bring it out;
if there were no one to crowd it out,
it could not burn itself.
Sentient beings are likewise;
although they possess the nature [of Buddhahood], because they lack the direct cause,
and if they do not encounter virtuous friends— the conditions for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to initiate their practice— [they cannot realize it].
The true Dharma cannot by itself eliminate afflictions or realize nirvana.
Regarding the use of perfuming (*vāsanā*),
the treatise itself explains:
This refers to the power of external conditions for sentient beings;
that is to say, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas realize Suchness and give rise to its functioning.
Gathering and transforming sentient beings to cause them to cultivate wholesome dharmas;
herein there are two parts.
First, the differentiated condition;
second, the equal condition.
As for the differentiated condition:
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"The practitioner relies upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood,
throughout that interval,
whether seen or heard.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas may appear as their kinsmen or as their teachers.
They may become friends, or servants, or enemies.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
through their compassion and skillful means, [act] toward these sentient beings.
They are gathered by means of the four methods of attraction,
which cause virtuous conduct to increase and lead them into the right path.
This refers to the condition of differentiation by name.
Within this differentiation,
there are those that are proximate and those that are remote.
Those that are near are swift;
those that are distant are long-lasting.
These are still merely manifestations of his response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Regarding "equal conditions," the treatise itself explains:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas..."
Having long ago made great vows,
they pledged to deliver all beings;
by the power of the habitual perfuming of these roots of goodness, [they attain this].
Spontaneously and constantly following all sentient beings,
he manifests himself according to their respective capacities for seeing and hearing.
This refers to manifesting the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body,
enabling all sentient beings to see the Buddha equally through the power of samādhi;
this is precisely the benefit of his true body.
The perfuming agent is as described above.
As for the "perfumable," it is as stated in the treatise:
There are two types of those who are perfumed.
First, those who are not yet associated [with the result], namely: ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
This causes one to practice with faith and compliance within the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness;
yet one has not yet been able to abandon delusion to correspond with reality.
Once these two have already corresponded, [one attains realization].
That is to say, it perfumes the supramundane Dharma-body of the Bodhisattva,
causing them to abandon the deluded mind and eliminate ignorance.
One realizes and witnesses suchness,
becoming in accord with the Dharma-body of the Buddha-Tathāgata,
free from all conceptual discrimination.
Relying solely on the power of the Dharma,
they naturally practice and proceed toward the ocean of the Buddha's wisdom.
The preceding section elucidates how the True [Mind] perfumes the deluded [mind], giving rise to pure dharmas.
Next, it clarifies how that deluded mind perfumes the True [Mind], producing pure dharmas.
Within this, there are two:
first, that which perfumes (the perfumer);
second, that which is perfumed (the perfumable).
Among the perfumers,
there are both general and specific types.
As for general perfuming:
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"Because there is a deluded mind, one feels weary of and seeks to leave behind birth and death."
In order to seek nirvana,
one perfumes the true mind and gains self-confidence in one's own nature.
It is solely True Suchness (tathatā).
Apart from Suchness, there are no phenomena;
these are merely what is seen through the deluded mind’s inversion.
Because one knows that external objects do not exist,
one practices various skillful means to cultivate conduct free from defilement that tends toward the truth.
Although there is that which is cultivated,
one does not grasp it nor dwell upon it,
due to the power of long-term cultivation.
Ignorance is then extinguished.
Because ignorance is extinguished,
the deluded mind does not arise.
Because the deluded mind does not arise,
the deluded objects follow suit,
and both the mind and its characteristics are exhausted.
This is called attaining nirvāṇa.
Because one has attained nirvāṇa, one spontaneously accomplishes inconceivable karmic functions that pervade the entire dharma-realm; such is the general characteristic.
Regarding "distinct perfuming," there are two explanations in the treatise: first,
the perfuming of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
This refers to ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and others who,
weary of the suffering of birth and death,
aspire toward nirvana.
Within these six consciousnesses,
through the practice of skillful means,
one perfumes and awakens the True [Nature].
Second is the perfuming of the mental intention,
which refers to bodhisattvas who perceive illusory phenomena.
There is nothing to be grasped or craved.
Knowing that the dharma of *tathatā* is quiescent and secure, they rouse their minds with vigor and proceed toward great *nirvāṇa*.
Within these seven consciousnesses,
one practices through skillful means to permeate and manifest the True [Nature].
It is simply because the deluded consciousness (*vāsanā-vijñāna*) can give rise to the objective consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
It is called "mind" (*manas*) because it is that upon which the arising of the objective consciousness depends;
it is not the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) within the objective consciousness itself.
The perfuming agent is thus.
There are two types of the perfumed:
first, that which is produced by perfuming.
First, it perfumes and generates the merit of the expedient means of the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha; second,
it perfumes and manifests the merit of the intrinsic purity of the nature of the *dharmakāya* Buddha.
Such is the mutual perfuming of the true and the false consciousnesses.
A question is asked:
How do the true and the false mutually perfume one another across time?
To address whether they exist at one and the same time,
the commentary states:
"Mutual perfuming must necessarily occur simultaneously."
What is the meaning of this?
It is that all phenomena of defilement and purity arise together through the coexistence of the real and the false.
The single reality does not arise;
delusion alone cannot be established. Why is this so?
Only the true exists, without falsehood.
The nature of truth is eternally serene;
because it is unconditioned and immutable, there is no arising or activity.
Since there is only delusion and no reality, the substance of delusion cannot be established; therefore, there is also no activity.
Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says:
"If there were no storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna)..."
The seven factors do not abide;
one does not plant suffering,
nor does one seek to weary of suffering while joyfully seeking nirvāṇa.
Only when truth and falsehood depend upon each other can they bring about the creation of all phenomena;
for they act in concert.
When phenomena are grasped according to emotional perceptions, they are all falsely constructed;
when phenomena are grasped according to their fundamental source,
they are all produced by the true mind.
It is like the various things one does in a dream;
these activities are subsumed under their secondary aspects,
for they are performed while in a state of昏睡 (muddled sleep).
The summary of matters follows from the root;
it is the result of what the mind has produced,
just as worldly people see a rope and perceive it as a snake.
The grasping of the snake follows from the delusion of the mind; it is the deluded mind that acts.
The grasping of the snake, when traced back to its source, is entirely the product of the rope.
All phenomena are like this.
Although reality is capable of producing [phenomena],
such production necessarily follows from conceptual construction,
just as a rope is perceived as a snake.
The snake arises from the emotion of darkness;
although delusion is capable of acting,
its action must rely upon the Real.
Just as one perceives a snake based on a rope,
the snake necessarily depends upon the rope;
yet true non-existence has no basis in perception.
The name is said to delusively permeate the Real;
the delusion arises from the Real.
The name is said to permeate the delusive.
In this manner, the principle of mutual perfuming has no sequence of before or after;
therefore, it is said to occur simultaneously.
Thus, the true and the false mutually perfume one another.
The essential point lies herein;
it should not fail to be recorded.
Next, we proceed to the mutual cognition between the real and the delusory.
To distinguish the perfuming:
as for the common characteristic consciousness,
it is the Buddha-nature’s true mind and the stage of ignorance.
These combine to form the fundamental consciousness,
named *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Based upon this, the *ādāna-vijñāna* arises through transformation, which is the mind that clings to a self.
Based on the fundamental transformation, the six consciousnesses—beginning with the visual consciousness—and the six faculties and objects arise;
this point has been explained above.
Now, based on these three, we shall clarify the process of mutual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
therein the crookedness [of the mind] is analyzed through three gates.
First, the characteristics of perfuming (*vāsanā*) are distinguished.
Second, the distinction between the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed object (*vāsyam*).
Third, the difference between that which undergoes perfuming and that which does not.
What is the characteristic of perfuming?
Now, this first clarifies the principle of mutual perfuming between the ādāna-vijñāna and the ālaya-vijñāna.
That ādāna, which is the mind that clings to a self,
perfumes the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna) to form the seeds of the self.
Once the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) has been perfumed by that ādāna, it is further able to induce the nature of self within that mind,
thereby producing the ādānavijñāna;
in this manner, they mutually perfume one another.
Their mutual interaction is inexhaustible;
thus, the *ādāna-vijñāna* and the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) stand to one another as cause and effect.
Question: By what means can this self be exhausted? Answer:
It is through hearing the teaching of non-self among the six consciousnesses and cultivating the understanding of non-self.
It perfumes the fundamental consciousness, forming the seeds of non-self;
the true mind within that fundamental [consciousness],
having received that perfuming, [becomes so].
It perfumes the fundamental ignorance, causing it to become thin;
because ignorance becomes thin,
the seeds of the self within ignorance are further thinned.
Because the seeds of the self are thin,
the arising of *dāna* (giving) occurs; thus,
the grasping for a self is also thin.
In this manner, they proceed in succession until all are exhausted.
Next, the six consciousnesses are correlated with the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) to clarify their mutual perfuming and activation.
Within those six consciousnesses,
defilement and purification arise;
such is the fault of the arising defilement.
It perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Within that fundamental consciousness, all dark natures and the nature of sensation are perfumed by defilement.
It becomes the seed of defilement.
Once the seed has been formed,
because ignorance is thick, [it continues].
It gives rise to the six consciousnesses;
within these six consciousnesses,
defilement and transgression further increase.
In this manner, they accumulate and habituate themselves without end.
The wholesome deeds cultivated within the six consciousnesses perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Within the fundamental consciousness,
the Buddha-nature and true mind are termed the "nature of liberation."
The nature of understanding receives the perfuming of those pure dharmas, thereby forming pure seeds.
Once these pure seeds have been formed,
they perfume ignorance.
Ignorance becomes attenuated;
because ignorance is attenuated,
the six consciousnesses arise in transformation.
Among the six consciousnesses,
wholesome transformation arises increasingly superior;
thus it proceeds successively until the ultimate limit is reached.
Thus, the six consciousnesses,
in relation to the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna),
serve as causes and effects for one another.
The treatise has thus concluded this first section.
Next, it clarifies the distinctions between the perfuming agent (*kṣobhaka*) and the perfumed object (*kṣobhya*).
The treatise states that, in brief, there are three types of perfuming agents.
The "infusion by a single word" is also termed in the treatise as "infusion by names.
There are two kinds of names.
First is the name of sound,
which is called the discrimination of names and words.
Second is the name of mind and speech.
It is said: "It is the discrimination of vitarka and vicāra.
Because ordinary beings follow after the names of all dharmas—the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth—they discriminate, grasp, and become attached to them."
It perfumes the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna),
forming the seeds of all phenomena such as the aggregates (skandha) and elements (dhātu).
Second is the perfuming of the view of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi).
By means of the ādāna-vijñāna and the mind of self-view within the six consciousnesses,
one perfumes the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna),
thereby forming the seeds of a self.
The perfuming of the three realms of existence consists of wholesome and unwholesome karma;
these are the causes of the three realms of existence.
It is called the "constituent of existence" (bhavāṅga),
for it is perfumed by wholesome and unwholesome karma within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
The formation of seeds of good and evil is called "perfuming with constituent parts" (*bhāgīya-vāsanā*).
Such is the nature of perfuming.
As for that which is called "perfumable," it is that which arises;
the treatise names its function as such.
Broadly categorized, there are four;
finely categorized, there are eleven.
As for the four broad categories:
The first is called "projecting and producing.
Once the fundamental consciousness has been perfumed by those wholesome, unwholesome, and other [states] to form seeds,
[the subsequent consciousness arises].
First, it draws forth those seeds to produce future fruits;
second, it is the retribution,
wherein the fundamental consciousness is perfumed by those wholesome, unwholesome, and other [states].
It transforms into the retributions of all suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
Third is the characteristic of the object-condition (*ālambana-nimitta*):
because the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is perfumed by that view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
It gives rise to the distinctions of "I" and "mine," and of self and other.
Fourth is its characteristic:
because the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is perfumed by those verbal expressions.
It arises with respect to all types of phenomena—whether the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; conditioned or unconditioned; internal or external.
Furthermore, it is divided into four [aspects], the first of which is consciousness resembling a self.
Within the appropriating consciousness (*ādāna-vijñāna*) and the six consciousnesses,
the self that is grasped does not exist,
yet it appears as if it exists.
Therefore, it is said that they resemble me,
like the body in a dream,
which has the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its substance through transformation.
This fundamental consciousness is called the "consciousness resembling a self.
Second is the "consciousness resembling the sense organs," namely the six sense organs, such as the eye and so forth.
That which is non-existent yet appears as existent is called a "semblance-faculty.
When the fundamental consciousness transforms into its own substance, this fundamental consciousness is termed the "semblance-faculty consciousness."
Third, consciousnesses resembling objects:
the six objects, such as form and so forth,
do not exist yet appear as if they do.
It is called "resembling the object.
The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) transforms itself as its substance;
thus, this fundamental consciousness is termed the "consciousness resembling the object" (*viṣayābhāsavijñāna*).
Fourth is the semblance of consciousness.
That ādāna and the six consciousnesses are not existent,
yet they appear as if they were existent.
That which resembles the existence imagined by ordinary beings is called "semblance-consciousness";
it has the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its substance through transformation.
This fundamental consciousness is called "consciousness resembling consciousness.
Such is the coarse classification;
the subtle classification consists of eleven types.
As stated in the treatise:
the first is body-consciousness,
which refers to the body consisting of the five sense faculties.
The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) transforms into its own substance;
this is the fundamental consciousness.
As for the "two bodies," the consciousness refers to the ādānavijñāna, the mind that clings to a self.
The fundamental consciousness transforms into its own substance;
this is the fundamental consciousness.
The consciousness of the three feelings is [the resultant consciousness].
The treatise states:
"That which is called 'mind' (manas) is the mind-faculty element (manas-indriya-dhātu)."
It universally presides over all sense objects;
its function of experiencing them is called "reception" (vedanā).

it is taught that there is false perfuming;
as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, the false perfumes the True.
What does it mean for there to be no perfuming?
If one says that within the True [Nature] pure dharmas are already perfected and do not require perfuming,
then the nature of the Dharma-Buddha is inherently present.
The essence of the Dharma may be said to be complete;
as for the nature of the Reward Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya-buddha*),
it has from the beginning only the sense of being capable of arising.
Since the essence of the phenomenon does not yet exist,
it is like a tree without a seed;
how can it be called "fulfilled"?
The Buddha-nature is fundamentally non-existent;
it exists only through provisional cultivation.
Why, then, do you not cultivate it?
Because the power of perfuming resides in the ultimate reality (tathatā), it is not definitively extinguished.
[The opponent] asks:
The natures of the real and the false are each distinct;
how, then, can they mutually permeate one another?
This has been explained above.
All that is cultivated arises from both the true and the delusive;
the cultivation is subsumed under the delusive.
All that is done through delusion is false;
all that is cultivated by embracing the truth is truly accomplished.
Although the True [Nature] is capable of acting,
its action necessarily follows delusion;
although delusion is capable of functioning, [it does so only through the True Nature].
It must necessarily rely on the True;
because the True and the False act together,
it is called "the True perfuming the False."
Because the false acts upon the true,
it is called "the false perfuming the true.
Within the false consciousness—
Having completed the treatment of these two gates,
next, regarding the true consciousness, the treatment of false attachments is presented according to the treatise.
There are two types of false attachments:
first, the attachment to a self held by ordinary persons;
second, the attachment to a self held by those of the Two Vehicles.
Question:
Ordinary worldlings also cling to all phenomena.
Why, then, is it specifically said that humans cling to the grasping of a self?
The commentary states:
Even subtle divisions are attached to all phenomena;
this is now addressed in contrast to the Two Vehicles.
Ordinary worldlings are attached to a self and to what belongs to a self;
this is collectively termed "clinging to persons."
Since all phenomena are subsumed within what belongs to the self,
they are discussed here in full according to their respective meanings, in accordance with the attachments of ordinary beings.
Briefly, there are two kinds:
first, the adherence to existence;
second, the adherence to non-existence.
Among those who cling to existence,
there are specifically four types.
The first is the clinging to [the self] as being real and identical to the spirit (ātman).
There are those who, upon hearing it said that the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the self,
claim it is identical to the "divine self" (ātman) grasped by non-Buddhists;
to counteract this attachment, [the following] is taught.
The Tathāgatagarbha is not the self,
nor a sentient being, nor a life-principle, nor a person.
Within the reality of the two attachments, it is fully endowed with both the pure and the defiled.
As Aśvaghoṣa said: "There are those who,
upon hearing it taught that the two dharmas of birth-and-death are the tathāgatagarbha,
immediately claim that birth-and-death are inherently present within reality."
To counteract this attachment,
it is taught that the tathāgatagarbha is pure by nature from the very beginning.
There are only the pure Buddha-dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
which are free from defilement.
If one were to say that within reality there truly exists birth and death, [it would be a misconception].
And to claim that such a person could realize awakening and forever leave behind birth and death—
this is impossible. If one says there exists a dharma-gate of the functioning of conditions through cultivation that accords with worldly phenomena, [it is likewise untenable].
It is not that this meaning does not exist;
there are three types of grasping at the mark of purity,
as Aśvaghoṣa said:
When some hear it said that within the Tathāgatagarbha all dharmas of merit are fully present, neither increasing nor decreasing,
they immediately claim that within the Truth (tattva) there exist form, mind, and so forth.
Regarding the distinction between self-characteristics,
it is taught as an antidote to this attachment that although the tathāgatagarbha is endowed with all dharmas, [it is not identical to them].
Based on true suchness (tathatā),
it is said that there are no marks of "this" and "that," no marks of "self" and "other," and even no marks of being apart from self and other.
In contrast to the defiled,
it is said that within that reality all phenomena are fully present;
furthermore, within that reality there are dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
They are of the same substance and arise through conditions; there is no distinction,
and one cannot apprehend any distinct characteristics.
The fourth concerns the grasping at a beginning and an end.
As Aśvaghoṣa said:
"There are those who, upon hearing it taught that birth and death arise based on the *tathāgatagarbha*, [misconceive this]."
Furthermore, they hear it said that because the Tathāgatagarbha gives rise to birth and death,
even though one attains nirvāṇa, one returns to give rise to birth and death;
and because birth and death arise, nirvāṇa has an end.
To counteract this clinging,
it is taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is without beginning and without end;
because it is without beginning, [it is without end].
Based on the arising of birth and death, there is no beginning to saṃsāra.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"If anyone were to proclaim that outside the three realms there is a further initial arising of sentient beings," [that would be a false view].
This is the teaching of non-Buddhists,
not the true Buddha-dharma,
because it lacks an end.
Based on this, one achieves nirvana;
yet nirvana has no end—
so some maintain.
Regarding those who maintain the view of non-existence:
there are some who proclaim that the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena constitutes true consciousness.
To counteract this clinging,
it is taught that [the nature] is truly not empty within this consciousness.
It is endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges.
Why is it called "empty"?
Therefore, it is said in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
It is the non-empty tathāgatagarbha.
The Nirvāṇa Sūtra also says:
"There is the tathāgatagarbha."
Although it is invisible,
once the afflictions have been destroyed,
one will certainly and inevitably attain it.
That text further states:
"If there are those who say that non-self, emptiness, and quiescence are the Tathāgatagarbha,
you should know this."
This person has long remained in birth and death,
enduring various sufferings for a great length of time,
and has not attained liberation.
Now, as for the statement in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* that "the Tathāgatagarbha is taught based on the doctrine of no-self," regarding this very Garbha:
It is called "empty" because it is devoid of what is falsely conceptualized;
it is not that the true Dharma is non-existent.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"In order to refute the non-Buddhists' attachment to a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*),
it is taught that all phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, are empty."
It is not that the reality as it is (yathābhūta) is empty apart from verbal expression.
This reality as it is is the sphere traversed by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
There is only the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and no other consciousnesses;
this is how one counteracts the false attachments of ordinary people.
Next, the counteractive measures for the false attachments of the two vehicles are explained.
This section contains two parts;
the first is the attachment to existence.
Persons of the two vehicles have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena;
they perceive the characteristics of birth-and-death and nirvana as being distinct.
Because of this insight,
one deeply fears birth and death and seeks to attain nirvana.
Delusion obscures suchness;
to counteract this clinging,
it is taught that "emptiness as it truly is" is free from all marks.
Birth-and-death is fundamentally quiescent, and nirvāṇa is likewise so;
the two types of grasping are definitively non-existent for those of the Two Vehicles.
Those with dull faculties perceive the emptiness of persons;
those with sharp faculties partially perceive the emptiness of phenomena.
They then take this emptiness to be the ultimate,
thereby obscuring and obstructing reality.
To counteract this attachment,
it is taught that [the nature of mind] is truly not empty and is endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges.
The eight consciousnesses are likewise so.
